subtype: Anger that is repeatedly hurting others [Observer]
passage:
Thursday night
Third time this month. Vasudha slammed her laptop shut in the design review, then threw a stapler that dented the wall right next to Kunal's head. Nobody said anything; everyone just stared at their screens. The new intern was shaking. I kept telling myself it's only stress, she's brilliant, she'll calm down. But this isn't a bad mood any more. People are scared of her.
After lunch I went to Meenakshi, our manager, and told her what I'd seen, including the stapler. She listened, thanked me, moved the intern to another desk that same afternoon, and said she'd speak to Vasudha tomorrow about safety and about seeing the company counsellor. I feel sick about it, but also relieved.
Jyoti

qa.q: What did Vasudha throw?
qa.a: A stapler, which dented the wall next to Kunal's head.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel after going to Meenakshi?
qa.a: Jyoti feels sick about it but also relieved, torn between loyalty to a colleague and everyone's safety.

qa.q: What did Meenakshi do in response?
qa.a: She listened, moved the intern to another desk that afternoon, and planned to talk to Vasudha about safety and seeing the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Meenakshi raises it?
qa.a: Vasudha may feel defensive or ashamed at first, but a counsellor could help her change the pattern.

grounding: A colleague sees repeated explosions and damage, realises it is more than a bad mood, and puts safety first by telling the manager.

passage:
Monday: Pema fell off the step and cried so hard she gulped air, hiccupped, then held her breath, face going red, before a huge sob. Parul panicked, jiggling her and saying, 'Stop, stop!' It took ages.
Wednesday: A bump on the knee. Pema began gulping again. This time Parul held her close against her chest and breathed slowly and deeply herself, humming.
Saturday: Pema's balloon popped. She gulped and hiccupped, then leaned into Parul's chest, and her small breaths slowly matched her mother's. The sobs faded.

qa.q: What happened on Saturday?
qa.a: Pema's balloon popped.

qa.q: How was Parul feeling on Monday when Pema held her breath?
qa.a: She felt panicked, jiggling Pema and saying 'Stop, stop!'

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Parul held Pema close and breathed slowly herself, so Pema's body could follow the calm.

qa.q: What might Pema have felt when Parul breathed slowly?
qa.a: Pema likely felt calmer and safer, her small breaths following Parul's.

grounding: Over a week a mother learns that holding her distressed toddler close and breathing slowly helps the child's breath settle.

passage: I'm Nilesh, Bhavna's big brother, and I watched Mumma teach her a game. Every evening when Bhavna was calm, they played 'smell the flower, blow the candle'. Bhavna sniffed a pretend flower slowly, then puffed at a pretend candle. Sometimes they blew bubbles through a straw, as slowly as possible. I thought it was silly. Then at the fair, Bhavna lost her balloon and started crying hard. I don't know what she was thinking, but she sniffed, blew one slow puff, then another. Mumma did it with her. After a few puffs her crying slowed down.

qa.q: What game did Mumma and Bhavna play?
qa.a: 'Smell the flower, blow the candle'.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been feeling when she lost her balloon?
qa.a: She was upset and sad, crying hard at losing the balloon.

qa.q: Why did practising when calm help at the fair?
qa.a: The slow-breathing game was already familiar, so Bhavna could reach for it when she got upset.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see the game after the fair?
qa.a: Nilesh probably no longer thinks it's silly, having seen it help his sister calm down.

grounding: A young child learns slow breathing as a game when calm and can reach for it when upset.

passage: Irawati, you say your breath goes fast when you're cross with your brother? Let your Vinita Aaji tell you something. When I was in Class 4, at our school in Nagpur, I had to recite a poem at assembly. My breath went quick and shallow, like a sparrow's, and my hands shook. When I was angry with my sister, the same thing: fast, fast, fast. My teacher, Kulkarni Bai, noticed. She put my hand on my belly and said, 'Make this rise slowly, and let the air out even slower, like cooling tea.' I tried it behind the curtain. My breath slowed, and so did my heart. I recited the whole poem. After that I knew my body would listen to me if I asked it gently.

qa.q: What did Kulkarni Bai tell young Vinita to do?
qa.a: Make the belly rise slowly and let the air out even slower, like cooling tea.

qa.q: How did young Vinita feel before reciting?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with quick, shallow breath and shaking hands.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
qa.a: The teacher noticing and teaching slow belly breathing, which calmed her body so she could recite the whole poem.

qa.q: How might Kulkarni Bai have felt watching Vinita recite?
qa.a: Kulkarni Bai was probably proud and pleased that the simple breathing had helped.

grounding: A grandmother recalls noticing her fast breath as a nervous schoolchild and learning that slow breathing quiets the body.

passage:
Sports teacher's note, inter-school meet, Saturday
After losing his 400-metre heat by a fraction, Raghav sat behind the stands crying hard and breathing very fast. Within a minute he said his fingers were tingling and his head was spinning, which frightened him more, and he breathed even faster. I knelt beside him, kept my voice slow and said, 'Breathe in gently, and out even longer, like blowing on hot soup.' I breathed with him. After a few minutes the tingling faded and he could sit up. He was embarrassed, so we talked privately. I've told his parents and suggested he mention it to his doctor at his next visit.
Tanuja

qa.q: What did Raghav say was happening to his fingers?
qa.a: They were tingling.

qa.q: Why did Raghav breathe even faster?
qa.a: The tingling and spinning head frightened him, so his fear grew and his breathing sped up more.

qa.q: What helped Raghav's sensations ease?
qa.a: Slowing down with a longer out-breath while Tanuja breathed with him in a calm voice.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt seeing Raghav's panic grow?
qa.a: Tanuja was likely concerned but steady, staying calm so Raghav could follow.

grounding: A teenager crying hard over-breathes and feels dizzy and tingly, and a longer out-breath eases the sensations.

passage: In the seminar room at the university in Buenos Aires, Mateo was next to present his thesis proposal. Selin, beside him, fidgeted with her notes and whispered how nervous she was. Mateo felt his own heart thumping. He stood, walked to the front and, before saying a word, let out a long, slow breath through his mouth. He dropped his shoulders, looked at the first slide and paused for a moment. Nobody noticed; to them he was just getting ready. His first sentence came out steady, and his voice stayed level even when the professor interrupted with a question. Afterwards Selin asked how he stayed so calm. 'One long breath out,' he said. 'Want to try it before yours?'

qa.q: What did Mateo do before saying a word?
qa.a: Let out a long, slow breath through his mouth.

qa.q: How was Mateo feeling as he stood up?
qa.a: He felt nervous, with his heart thumping.

qa.q: Why did Mateo's small routine work?
qa.a: The slow exhale and dropped shoulders steadied his voice and thinking, quietly, without anyone noticing.

qa.q: How might Selin feel when Mateo offers to share the trick?
qa.a: Selin probably feels relieved and grateful, hoping it will steady her own nerves.

grounding: A student slows the exhale, drops the shoulders and pauses before presenting, steadying voice and thinking unnoticed.

passage: With the quarterly report due at five and the office internet dropping every ten minutes, Vidya hunched over her laptop in the Gurugram office. By three her neck ached, her jaw was tight and she felt oddly drained. Pranav, at the next desk, said, 'You just held your breath the whole time that page loaded.' Vidya realised he was right. She'd been breathing high and shallow all afternoon, sometimes not at all. She sat back, dropped her shoulders and took five slow breaths, longer on the way out. The connection was still unreliable, but her head cleared. She set a reminder to check her breathing every hour and finished the report by quarter to five.

qa.q: What did Pranav notice Vidya doing?
qa.a: Holding her breath the whole time the page loaded.

qa.q: How was Vidya feeling by three o'clock?
qa.a: She felt tense and oddly drained, with an aching neck and a tight jaw.

qa.q: What did Vidya do to reset her body?
qa.a: She sat back, dropped her shoulders, took five slow breaths with longer out-breaths, and set an hourly reminder.

qa.q: How might Pranav see the moment?
qa.a: Pranav was probably concerned in a friendly way and glad to point out something Vidya hadn't noticed.

grounding: A stressed worker holds her breath and breathes high in the chest under a deadline, and a few deliberate slow breaths reset her.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was a GOOD day. It rained all week and we were stuck indoors, and I was so grumpy I fought with Imran over the TV remote three times. Last night I couldn't even sleep properly. Today the sun came out and Ammi sent us to the park. Imran and I raced to the big tree ten times, played catch and rolled down the grassy slope till we were dizzy. When we came home I did all my maths without a single fight. Ammi said, 'See what running does?' Even Imran was nice. Tomorrow Ms Pinto wants to keep us in at games time to finish our project. I'm going to ask her if we can finish it after school instead.
Reena

qa.q: How many times did Reena and Imran race to the big tree?
qa.a: Ten times.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after the week stuck indoors?
qa.a: Reena felt grumpy and restless, fighting with Imran and sleeping badly.

qa.q: Why is it sensible for Reena to ask Ms Pinto to keep games time?
qa.a: Physical play helps Reena's mood and focus, so taking it away could make work and behaviour worse, not better.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the change after the park?
qa.a: Ammi likely felt pleased and relieved, seeing running bring back peace and focus.

grounding: A child who runs and plays outdoors sleeps and behaves better, and physical play is part of how children regulate feelings.

passage: Joining the school kabaddi team in Class 9 was the best thing I did. I used to dread Mondays; now I'd come home from practice tired but calm, and sleep like a stone. The team became my people. Uma, our captain, waited for me at the gate every evening. Then in Class 10 we reached the district finals, and everything changed. The coach started weighing us every week and shouting about 'looking like athletes'. I began skipping lunch and lying awake before matches, sick with worry about losing. Uma noticed. 'Swati, this was supposed to be the fun part.' We told our PE teacher about the weighing, and she spoke to the coach that same day.

qa.q: Who waited for Swati at the gate every evening?
qa.a: Uma, the captain.

qa.q: How did Swati feel before matches in Class 10?
qa.a: Swati felt sick with worry about losing and pressured about looking a certain way, lying awake at night.

qa.q: What did Swati and Uma do about the weighing?
qa.a: They told their PE teacher, who spoke to the coach that same day.

qa.q: What might Uma have felt noticing Swati's change?
qa.a: Uma probably felt worried and protective, missing the fun they used to share.

grounding: A teenager gains energy, calm and friends from a team sport until pressure to win and to look a certain way turns it into stress.

passage: It had rained for four days in Pune, and Chinmay had spent the whole Sunday hunched over his desk and phone. By evening he snapped at his little brother, slammed his book and groaned at every question. His mother, Avni, noticed his jiggling knee and the way he kept rubbing his neck. She didn't lecture. When the rain paused around six, she tied her shoes and said, 'I'm walking to the lake before it starts again. Come keep me company?' He rolled his eyes, but came. They walked fast, dodging puddles, hardly talking. By the time they reached the bhel stall, he was joking about the frogs. The rain came back on the way home, and they ran the last stretch, laughing.

qa.q: Where did Avni say she was walking?
qa.a: To the lake, before the rain started again.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she saw Chinmay's jiggling knee?
qa.a: Avni felt concerned, sensing that hours of sitting had made him restless and snappy.

qa.q: Why did Avni's invitation work better than an order?
qa.a: Offering the walk as company, not a command, let Chinmay join without losing face, and the movement lifted his mood.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel by the time they reached the bhel stall?
qa.a: He felt lighter and cheerful, joking about the frogs.

grounding: A parent sees a teenager snappy after long sitting and offers a walk as company, and movement lifts his mood.
